title: the departure
hook: bark clothes are brought out, Sita doesn't know how to put them on, and Lakshmana's mother gives him one verse

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure, part one. Gifts for everyone, and an old man's staff flying across the river. Did you give something away? Today, the goodbyes, and the end of a week. Day five hundred thirty-two.

Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk to the palace on foot. Crowds line the streets, and Valmiki lets us hear them. People who cheered for the coronation a day ago are weeping now, and some are openly criticizing the king. Inside, the whole family is waiting: the old king, three queens, counselors, priests. This is the last room before the road. And someone has brought a pile of clothes made of tree bark.
screen: `THEY WALK TO THE PALACE.` → `THE CROWDS WEEP.` → `A PILE OF BARK CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha begs Rama, one last time, to stay just one night. Rama gently refuses. The king orders the army and the treasury to go with him. Kaikeyi objects, and Rama himself turns it down: why keep the rope, he asks, once you've given away the elephant? Then Kaikeyi hands out the bark garments. Rama and Lakshmana take off their fine clothes and put them on. Sita takes one, and stands holding it, confused. She has never worn anything like it. Valmiki tells us she doesn't know how to tie it, and tries, and can't, and is ashamed, and starts to cry. Rama ties it for her, over her silk. It's one of the tenderest moments in the book. Vasishtha, watching, finally loses his temper with Kaikeyi. Sita was never part of the boons, he says. She doesn't need to wear bark. And the king orders that Sita be given clothes and jewels enough for all fourteen years. Then the mothers speak. Kausalya counsels Sita. And Sumitra, Lakshmana's mother, gives her son one verse, which many people know by heart: rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi māṃ viddhi janakātmajām, ayodhyām aṭavīṃ viddhi, gaccha tāta yathāsukham. Think of Rama as your father Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya. Go, my child, and be at peace. Look back at this week. Sita argued and won. Lakshmana raged, then held back, then took up a spade. Gifts were given. And now a mother sends her son into exile by telling him he isn't leaving home at all.
screen: `STAY ONE NIGHT. NO.` · `SITA CAN'T TIE THE BARK.` · `VASISHTHA: SITA WASN'T IN THE BOONS.` · `SUMITRA: THE FOREST IS AYODHYA.` · then, large: `RĀMAṂ DAŚARATHAṂ VIDDHI.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Sumitra told her son: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Try it with wherever you are. On a breath in, notice this room, this chair, this light. On a breath out, let it be home for these two minutes, nothing to escape from, nothing missing. If your mind goes to somewhere else you'd rather be, gently bring it back here, and call this home again. The bell holds the time.
The departure, part two: the goodbyes. Bark clothes, Rama tying Sita's, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya.
Your line: the departure. Today, wherever you end up, try calling it home for a minute. Day five hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Sumitra's verse, rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi, is often recited in Hindu homes and quoted in talks on the Ramayana as a picture of how to make any place home.

fork.setup: you're Sumitra. your son is leaving for fourteen years in the forest with his brother. what do you tell him?
options: come back as soon as you can.
think of Rama as your father, Sita as me, the forest as Ayodhya.
fork.reveal: her verse tells him he isn't leaving home: home goes with him.

original.note: Sanskrit valkala: bark, and clothing made of bark, worn by forest ascetics.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sumitra just says goodbye.
what it means: she tells Lakshmana that Rama is his father, Sita his mother and the forest his home.
what a scholar hears: some commentators also read the verse a second way, with Rama as Vishnu and Sita as Lakshmi, so that the forest becomes heaven itself.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 34–38 (farewell to the king; the army refused; bark garments; Vasishtha rebukes Kaikeyi)
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 40.9 (Sumitra to Lakshmana)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm, especially Sumitra's verse (40.9 in many printed editions; 39 in others).
Confirm the transliteration of Sumitra's verse; the English is the script's own rendering.
The elephant-and-rope saying: confirm wording and that Rama, not another speaker, says it.
Vasishtha's rebuke and the king's order of clothes and jewels for Sita: confirm.
The second (devotional) reading of the verse is attributed to commentators generally; confirm.
